title: An Energy-Efficient Kalman Filter Architecture with Tunable Accuracy for Brain-Computer Interfaces
problem: Kalman Filters are standard for BCIs to predict motion from brain activity, but hardware implementations specialized for embedded BCI constraints (latency-accuracy tuning, energy efficiency) are lacking.
method: A configurable KF hardware architecture with tunable latency and accuracy parameters enables design-space exploration for BCI applications; integrated as accelerators into a heterogeneous SoC, supporting efficient neural data processing with dynamic parameter adjustment.

title: Late Breaking Results: Source-Aware Adaptive Cache Management for CXL-enabled Disaggregated Memory Sharing
problem: CXL-enabled disaggregated memory systems with multiple hosts exhibit changing access patterns; conventional cache policies cannot track per-host behavior, making it difficult to optimize shared memory efficiency.
method: Alchemy system jointly optimizes cache replacement and bypassing policies using reinforcement learning with source-aware adaptivity. It runs as an online RL agent that tracks per-host access patterns. Rewards derive from sampling-based action effectiveness and per-host macro-level performance metrics.

title: Forecasting GPU Performance for Deep Learning Training and Inference
problem: Predicting GPU performance for deep learning workloads on unseen GPU models (new GPU on existing model, or existing model on new GPU) is inaccurate with prior ML-based approaches, which attempt to predict end-to-end kernel latency directly and suffer >100% error on new model-GPU pairs.
method: NeuSight decomposes a single DL kernel prediction into smaller working sets called 'tiles' that correspond to the GPU's SM-level execution granularity. Tile-granularity predictions are made by a learned ML model, then aggregated across tiles to estimate end-to-end latency. The approach is bounded by fundamental performance laws (roofline model) and incorporates both GPU hardware parameters and software library optimizations (cuDNN, cuBLAS heuristics) to constrain the prediction space, enabling generalization to unseen GPUs by parameterizing hardware characteristics rather than encoding GPU identity.

title: Criticality-Aware Instruction-Centric Bandwidth Partitioning for Data Center Applications
problem: Co-locating latency-critical (LC) and best-effort (BE) tasks on shared datacenter nodes causes memory bandwidth contention that results in priority inversion, where BE tasks monopolize bandwidth and cause LC tasks to violate quality-of-service (QoS) requirements.
method: Pivot is a bandwidth partitioning system that prioritizes LC memory accesses at every component along the full memory path (L1/L2/L3 caches, DRAM controller) rather than at a single bottleneck point. Critically, Pivot selectively prioritizes only performance-critical loads—those causing long stalls on the re-order buffer (ROB)—rather than all LC accesses. A two-phase profiling technique identifies these critical loads offline with minimal runtime overhead: Phase 1 profiles whole-execution hit/miss behavior per load PC, and Phase 2 uses those profiles to tag critical loads for hardware prioritization during production runs.

title: SWIPER: Minimizing Fault-Tolerant Quantum Program Latency via Speculative Window Decoding
problem: Parallel window decoding for fault-tolerant quantum error correction requires some decoding tasks to be delayed until preceding windows complete, creating head-of-line blocking that inflates program runtime, especially during T gate teleportation where decoding latency directly extends logical circuit depth.
method: SWIPER introduces a speculative window decoder inspired by classical branch prediction. A lightweight speculation step predicts data dependencies between adjacent decoding windows, allowing multiple layers of decoding tasks to begin simultaneously rather than waiting for dependency resolution. If speculation is wrong, the decoder rolls back and re-decodes; the state-of-the-art compilation pipeline ensures that speculation opportunities are maximized. Performance is evaluated using a detailed open-source cycle-accurate simulator.

title: Mascot: Predicting Memory Dependencies and Opportunities for Speculative Memory Bypassing
problem: Memory dependence prediction (MDP) and speculative memory bypassing (SMB) require conflicting predictor properties: MDP tolerates false positives but not false negatives, while SMB tolerates false negatives but not false positives. Prior TAGE-based predictors for either mechanism fail to learn patterns of non-dependence, causing inaccuracy.
method: Mascot is a TAGE-inspired predictor that learns both dependence and non-dependence contexts. Unlike prior designs that only learn dependence patterns, Mascot tracks the history of non-aliasing outcomes in the TAGE table entries, enabling low false negative rates required for MDP and low false positive rates required for SMB from a single shared structure. The predictor is used in two modes: MDP-only (for load issue gating) and combined MDP+SMB (for value forwarding from store to load bypassing address resolution).

title: CREST-CiM: Cross-Coupling-Enhanced Differential STT-MRAM for Robust Computing-in-Memory in Binary Neural Networks
problem: Standard MRAM-based computing-in-memory suffers from low distinguishability of stored weights (+1/-1), resulting in poor sense-margin and vulnerability to process variations and hardware non-idealities.
method: CREST-CiM uses two cross-coupled magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) per bitcell to store complementary weights (+1 and -1), enhancing the high-to-low current ratio to 8100. Cross-coupling improves differential sensing and margin.

title: Hardware-aware Calibration Protocol for Quantum Computers
problem: Quantum computer calibration—optimizing control parameters to ensure accurate gate implementation—does not account for physical qubit heterogeneity, and existing methods serialize calibration operations, causing excessive calibration overhead and suboptimal gate fidelity as qubit counts scale.
method: The protocol operates in two stages. First, a profiling phase evaluates qubit-pair responses to different waveform candidates, then assigns one of three calibration policies to each pair based on the profiling data (hardware-aware, fine-grained policy selection). Second, a graph-traversal algorithm identifies sets of compatible (non-interfering) calibration operations that can execute in parallel, converting the sequential calibration schedule into a parallel one. The protocol was validated on real IBM quantum hardware with up to 127 qubits.

title: Efficient Optimization with Encoded Ising Models
problem: Ising solvers (quantum, oscillator-based, and probabilistic computers) must include penalty terms to enforce constraints for combinatorial optimization problems, causing solvers to spend the majority of compute time exploring infeasible states and often failing to find any feasible solution.
method: The Encoded Ising Model (E-I model) extends the standard Ising model by inserting a digital encoding circuit between the solver and the energy landscape, restricting the search space to only feasible states without penalty terms. The Fuse software framework provides a high-level API to describe such constrained functions and automatically lowers them to a p-computer target. The encoding circuit uses a combinational logic layer that maps solver spin states to legal variable assignments, reducing the fraction of iterations spent on infeasible solutions by orders of magnitude.

title: HSMU-SpGEMM: Achieving High Shared Memory Utilization for Parallel Sparse General Matrix-Matrix Multiplication on Modern GPUs
problem: Hash-based SpGEMM algorithms on GPUs fail to simultaneously minimize hash collisions and efficiently utilize fast shared memory, causing significant performance degradation when executing sparse general matrix-matrix multiplication.
method: HSMU-SpGEMM introduces a novel accumulator design that maximizes shared memory utilization on modern GPUs by rethinking the hash-based accumulation strategy to reduce collision overhead while packing more active data into shared memory. The approach also optimizes the symbolic stages of SpGEMM (row count, product computation) to complement the new accumulator. Evaluation is performed on three GPU microarchitectures (Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Turing).

title: Architecting Space Microdatacenters: A System-level Approach
problem: There is no principled cost-aware methodology for architecting server-based computing systems deployed on low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites (Space Microdatacenters, SuDC). Prior work proposes the concept but does not model Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) to guide hardware design decisions.
method: The authors build a TCO model for SuDC that decomposes costs into compute power, mass, monetary hardware cost, and communication. They perform a design space exploration over heterogeneous accelerator configurations (high FLOPs/W devices), collaborative compute constellations (EO satellites with onboard accelerators), monolithic vs. distributed architectures, and compute overprovisioning strategies. TCO sensitivity analysis reveals power dominates sublinearly; monetary cost and mass are secondary.

title: DPUaudit: DPU-assisted Pull-based Architecture for Near-Zero Cost System Auditing
problem: Existing hardware-based system auditing frameworks offload log processing to isolated hardware but still suffer high runtime overhead (>10% slowdown) because they use a push-based architecture requiring a log sender to run on the monitored host, which necessitates heavy software protection mechanisms that consume significant CPU resources.
method: DPUaudit replaces the push-based log sender on the monitored host with a pull-based architecture using a DPU (Data Processing Unit/SmartNIC) to actively pull system events directly from the monitored host's memory over the network interconnect. By removing the log sender from the monitored host entirely, DPUaudit eliminates the need for complex software protection mechanisms guarding it, achieving near-zero overhead. The DPU handles log collection, processing, and integrity verification in an isolated SmartNIC environment, physically separated from the monitored host.

title: DReX: Accurate and Scalable Dense Retrieval Acceleration via Algorithmic-Hardware Codesign
problem: Approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) used in RAG dense retrieval is dataset-specific and inherently low-recall, causing irrelevant or incomplete context to degrade LLM generation quality. Exact nearest-neighbor search is too compute- and bandwidth-intensive for conventional processors.
method: DReX combines two hardware tiers: in-DRAM logic performs early filtering by comparing query vectors against embedding centroids to eliminate distant candidates without moving full vectors off-chip, and an outside-DRAM near-memory accelerator then executes exact k-NN search on the filtered, much smaller candidate set. The in-DRAM filter exploits processing-in-memory (PIM) capabilities of commodity DRAM to compute approximate distance bounds, bypassing DRAM-to-processor transfers for the bulk of vectors. This two-stage pipeline minimizes off-chip data movement while guaranteeing exact retrieval on the survivors.

title: Enhancing LLM-based Quantum Code Generation with Multi-Agent Optimization and Quantum Error Correction
problem: LLM-based quantum code generation struggles with fault-tolerance and correctness; general-purpose LLM techniques (CoT, RAG) don't translate to quantum domain without domain-specific optimization.
method: Multi-agent framework where each agent targets specific quantum optimizations (error correction, circuit synthesis); semantic analyzer with multi-pass inference; integrates structured Chain-of-Thought and error correction decoder; test suite measuring per-agent contribution.

title: CTXNL: A Software-Hardware Co-designed Solution for Efficient CXL-Based Transaction Processing
problem: Directly adopting CXL for multi-node transaction processing incurs high performance overhead because standard CXL cache coherence primitives enforce fine-grained coherence uniformly, while transactional data has loosely coherent access patterns that do not require full coherence at every access.
method: CTXNL is a software-hardware co-designed system that introduces a hybrid coherence primitive tailored to the transactional access pattern. The core mechanism allows transaction developers to selectively opt in or out of cache coherence on a per-data-item basis, bypassing full CXL coherence overhead for data items that are only loosely coherent during normal transaction execution while maintaining correctness via selective coherence enforcement at commit or conflict points. Hardware support is added to CXL memory controllers to efficiently implement the selective coherence primitive.

title: SpecASan: Mitigating Transient Execution Attacks Using Speculative Address Sanitization
problem: Transient execution attacks (Spectre, Meltdown, MDS) exploit speculative execution to leak sensitive data through residual microarchitectural state, and existing defenses either delay speculative execution or require costly shadow structures and dynamic information flow tracking. Providing strong security against transient execution attacks without significant performance overhead remains an open problem.
method: SpecASan extends ARM's Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) from the committed path to the speculative path. When a speculative memory access fails the MTE tag comparison (i.e., the tag on the pointer does not match the tag in memory), that access is stalled until speculation resolves, preventing it from affecting microarchitectural state (caches, TLBs). This is combined with existing Control-Flow Integrity (CFI) enforcement to block gadget construction. The approach models transient execution attacks as software-defined security contract violations and enforces the contracts in hardware using existing MTE tag-check hardware, requiring minimal new hardware.
